title: The Framework: A Repeatable Structure So You Never Freeze
tagline: Every strong candidate follows roughly the same script. Internalize it and the open-ended question stops being scary.
summary: The 7-step structure that turns a vague prompt into a confident answer.

paragraphs: A system design interview is deliberately open-ended: 'Design Twitter.' With no structure, candidates freeze, jump straight to databases, or ramble. With a structure, you always know what to do next — which keeps you calm and makes you look senior.

The framework below has many names (RESHADED, the 4-step, the 7-step) but they're all the same idea: **start broad and abstract, get agreement, then progressively go deeper into the parts that matter.** You drive; the interviewer steers.

blocks.title: It's a conversation, not a monologue
blocks.text: The framework gives you a default path, but the interviewer will interrupt to probe areas they care about. That's good — follow their lead. The structure is your safety net for when they go quiet, not a script to recite over their objections.

items.title: Requirements & scope (3–5 min)
items.detail: Clarify functional requirements (what it does), non-functional requirements (scale, latency, availability, consistency), and explicitly state what's out of scope. Never start designing until you've agreed on scope.

items.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation (2–4 min)
items.detail: Estimate QPS, storage, and bandwidth. This justifies later choices (caching, sharding) with numbers instead of hand-waving. Skip it only if the interviewer says so.

items.title: API design (2–3 min)
items.detail: Define the core endpoints / method signatures. This pins down exactly what the system does and the client-server contract before you draw boxes.

items.title: Data model (3–5 min)
items.detail: What are the main entities, and what storage do they need? Make the SQL-vs-NoSQL call here, justified by the access patterns you just defined.

items.title: High-level design (5–10 min)
items.detail: Draw the boxes: clients → load balancer → services → databases/caches/queues. Walk the main flows end to end. Get the interviewer to agree this is reasonable before going deeper.

items.title: Deep dive (10–15 min)
items.detail: Zoom into 1–2 of the most interesting/critical components — the part that's actually hard (the fan-out, the hot shard, the consistency boundary). This is where senior signal lives.

items.title: Wrap up: bottlenecks & trade-offs (3–5 min)
items.detail: Identify single points of failure, scaling bottlenecks, and the trade-offs you made. Mention what you'd monitor and how you'd evolve it. Strong finishers revisit the original requirements.

blocks.text: Say the steps out loud at the start: 'I'll clarify requirements, do some quick estimates, sketch the APIs and data model, draw a high-level design, then deep-dive the tricky parts.' Announcing your plan instantly signals experience and buys you thinking room.

blocks.title: The #1 time mistake
blocks.text: Spending 20 minutes perfecting the high-level boxes and never reaching a deep dive. The deep dive is where you differentiate yourself. Keep the high-level design deliberately fast and 'good enough', then go deep. If you're running long, say 'let me move to the interesting part' and jump.

sections.title: The mental model: breadth then depth

blocks.caption: Always move from abstract agreement to concrete detail — never the reverse.

items.detail: Establish the big picture and get buy-in before adding detail. Diving into a specific database schema before agreeing on requirements is the classic junior mistake.
Every design decision should trace back to a requirement or an estimate. 'It's read-heavy (100:1), so I'll add a cache' is gold. 'I'll add Redis because everyone does' is not.
There's rarely one right answer. Saying 'I'll choose X over Y because we prioritized availability over consistency here' shows engineering maturity — the thing they're really grading.

cheatsheet: 7 steps: Requirements → Estimation → API → Data model → High-level design → Deep dive → Trade-offs.
Announce your plan up front — it signals experience and buys thinking time.
Always go breadth-first then depth: align on scope before drawing, draw before deep-diving.
Budget time: keep high-level design fast; the deep dive is where you earn senior signal.
Every decision must trace to a requirement or an estimate — never 'because everyone uses it'.
Finish by naming SPOFs, bottlenecks, trade-offs, and how you'd monitor/evolve the system.
It's a conversation: the interviewer steers, you drive — follow their probes.

questions.prompt: The interviewer says 'Design Instagram.' What are the first words out of your mouth, and why?
questions.hint: Don't start designing. Don't start with a database.
answer: The first thing is to *not* start designing. I'd say something like: 'Before I design anything, let me clarify scope and requirements so we build the right thing.' Then I'd ask functional questions — are we focusing on posting photos and viewing a feed? Do we need stories, direct messages, search? — and non-functional questions — roughly how many users/DAU, is this read-heavy (it is), what's our latency target, do we prioritize availability or consistency for the feed?

I'd then narrow scope explicitly: 'Let's focus on uploading photos and the home feed, and treat DMs and stories as out of scope.' Only after we've agreed on that would I move to estimation and design. Opening this way matters because the question is intentionally vague; jumping straight to 'I'll use Postgres and S3' signals that I design before I understand the problem, which is the exact opposite of the senior behavior they're grading for.
keyPoints: State scope and what's explicitly out of scope
followUps: The interviewer says 'assume 500M users.' What do you do with that number next?

questions.prompt: You're 25 minutes in and still polishing the high-level boxes. The interviewer seems restless. What do you do?
questions.hint: Recognize the time trap; the deep dive is what differentiates you.
answer: I'd recognize I've fallen into the most common time trap — over-investing in the high-level diagram and starving the deep dive, which is where the real signal is. I'd proactively say: 'This high-level design is solid enough; let me move to the most interesting/challenging part.' Then I'd pick the component that's genuinely hard for this system — for Instagram that might be feed generation and the fan-out strategy, or handling a celebrity's millions of followers — and dive deep there.

Taking that initiative is itself a positive signal: it shows time-awareness and judgment about where complexity lives. Restlessness from the interviewer usually means 'I've seen enough of the obvious stuff; show me you can handle the hard part.' Reading that cue and steering toward depth — rather than continuing to refine boxes everyone already agrees on — is exactly what separates a strong candidate from one who runs out of time with nothing deep to show.
keyPoints: Proactively pivot: 'let me move to the interesting part'
Pick the genuinely hard component to deep-dive
Reading the interviewer's cue and steering is positive signal
followUps: Which component would you choose to deep dive for a chat app, and why that one?
